content: The Mumbai plague epidemic was a devastating outbreak of bubonic plague that struck the city of Mumbai (then Bombay) in the late 19th century. This epidemic resulted in the deaths of thousands of people and caused a significant exodus of residents, leading to a sharp decline in the city’s population. Causes The rapid expansion of Bombay’s commercial activities attracted a large influx of workers to the city. By the 1891 census, the population of Bombay had reached 820,000. Over 70% of these immigrant workers lived in overcrowded and unsanitary chawls (tenement housing). The city’s infrastructure and public services were ill-equipped to support this growing population, particularly in the slums, where various diseases were endemic. Detection In September 1896, the first case of bubonic plague in Bombay was identified in Mandvi by Dr. Acacio Gabriel Viegas. The disease spread rapidly throughout the city, with the death toll reaching an estimated 1,900 people per week by the end of the year. The epidemic prompted a mass exodus from Bombay, and by the 1901 census, the city’s population had decreased to 780,000. Dr. Viegas accurately diagnosed the disease as bubonic plague and provided care to patients despite the significant personal risk involved. He also initiated a vigorous campaign to clean up the slums and eradicate rats, which were the primary carriers of the plague. To validate his findings, four independent teams of experts were brought in, and their confirmation of his diagnosis led the Governor of Bombay to invite Dr. Waldemar Haffkine, a scientist who had previously developed a cholera vaccine, to create a vaccine for the plague. Response In the first year of the epidemic, a research laboratory was established at J.J. Hospital. By 1899, this laboratory was relocated to the Government House in Parel under the direction of Dr. Haffkine, marking the foundation of the Haffkine Institute. Wealthier residents sought to escape the plague by moving to the city’s northern suburbs, an effort supported by industrialist Jamsetji Tata, who worked to open up these areas for settlement. However, the brunt of the epidemic was borne by mill workers and the urban poor. The health department’s anti-plague measures included police searches, the isolation of infected individuals, the detention of travelers in camps, and the forced evacuation of residents from certain parts of the city. These measures were widely perceived as intrusive and distressing, compounding the fear and anxiety caused by the plague itself. Mortality and Public Health In 1900, the mortality rate from the plague was approximately 22 per thousand. For comparison, the mortality rates for tuberculosis, cholera, and other febrile illnesses were 12, 14, and 22 per thousand, respectively. While the plague was particularly feared due to its contagious nature, other diseases claimed a comparable or even greater toll on the population. Urban Improvements On December 9, 1898, the Bombay City Improvement Trust (CIT) was established by an act of the British Parliament. The CIT was tasked with creating a healthier urban environment. One of its initiatives was the construction of roads, such as Princess Street and Sydenham Road (now Mohammed Ali Road), designed to channel fresh sea air into the densely populated areas of the city.
